LOS ALAMOS NATIONAL LABORATORY / NUMERICAL ALGORITHMS

More realistic simulations. Far less repeated computation.

Why this matters

Machine-learned models can predict how atoms interact, but the electric charges in a material also respond to atoms far away. Computing that response typically means solving a costly global problem at every simulation step. Approximating charge response without a consistent energy-and-force formulation can compromise physical accuracy and long-time numerical stability.

My research at Los Alamos National Laboratory tackles both problems: accelerate the global charge calculation, then verify the simulation still gets the physics right. I developed a charge-conserving GPU solver, built the multiscale ALAMOS preconditioner, and advanced it to ALAMOS-0. In our 104,640-atom run, ALAMOS-0 eliminated corrective Krylov iterations while keeping energy fluctuations bounded. The charge-response work accounted for less than 10% of runtime, bringing the cost closer to a fixed-charge model while still allowing charges to respond to their environment.

01 / EXPLORE THE RESEARCH

From the original GMRES baseline to PPCG, ALAMOS, and ALAMOS-0.

The original Shadow MD implementation used diagonally preconditioned GMRES to compute charge-response corrections. I developed a GPU-accelerated, charge-conserving projected preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PPCG) solver, then created local and full ALAMOS preconditioners before advancing to ALAMOS-0, which eliminated corrective Krylov iterations in our large-scale test. The chart shows how solver work accumulates over time, while the panel alongside it shows the average iterations per MD step and the corresponding total work.

02 / WHAT I DEVELOPED

How I got from fewer iterations to none.

I first derived a GPU charge-conserving solver, then invented ALAMOS to reduce its iterative work. ALAMOS-0 goes further: our 104,640-atom validation required no corrective Krylov iterations across 200,000 integration steps.

01 / THE FIRST CONTRIBUTIONGPU

A charge-conserving solver.

Before ALAMOS, my first step was deriving and GPU-implementing projected preconditioned conjugate gradient (PPCG), a charge-conserving Krylov solver that replaces the earlier GMRES + diagonal baseline while enforcing the total-charge constraint exactly.

PPCG · THE FIRST STEP BEYOND THE BASELINEGMRES + diagonal → charge-conserving projected preconditioned CG on GPU
What makes it different?

The solver projects every correction into the charge-neutral subspace, preserving the global charge constraint while allowing standard preconditioning and matrix-vector operations.

02 / THE EARLIER STEPALAMOS

ALAMOS cut the Krylov workload dramatically.

After PPCG, I developed ALAMOS as a multiscale approximation to the electronic response. At the same strict tolerance, PPCG + full ALAMOS averaged 3.06 iterations per step versus 23.47 for the original GMRES + diagonal baseline, an 87% reduction. That earlier ALAMOS result is the bridge between my projected preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PPCG) solver and the later ALAMOS-0 zero-correction result.

STRICT RMS · −87% VS GMRESPPCG + full ALAMOS · 52,320 atoms · 10⁻⁵ RMS · Fig. 3
13× FEWER VS GMRESGMRES + diagonal (12.9) → PPCG + full ALAMOS (1.0) · 10⁻³ RMS · Fig. 3
How does it compare with GMRES?

At 10⁻³ RMS, diagonal-GMRES averaged 12.9 iterations per MD step; PPCG with full ALAMOS averaged 1.0, a 13× reduction. At the stricter 10⁻⁵ RMS tolerance, GMRES averaged 23.47 iterations versus 3.06 with PPCG + full ALAMOS, a reduction of approximately 87%. The separate ALAMOS-0 stability test then completed 200,000 steps with no corrective Krylov iterations.

03 / THE BIGGER STEP · ALAMOS-0ALAMOS-0

Zero Krylov iterations. 104,640 atoms.

I then pushed the idea further: instead of using ALAMOS to help an iterative solver converge, ALAMOS-0 applies the preconditioner directly. The 104,640-atom simulation completed 200,000 steps (100 ps) without corrective Krylov iterations and showed no systematic energy drift in the reported interval.

0 ITERATIONS · 100% OF TESTED STEPSALAMOS-0 · 200,000 steps · Fig. 7 · NVIDIA A100
CHARGE WORK · 0.09 μs/atom/stepALAMOS-0 · 104,640-atom NVE run · Fig. 7 · NVIDIA A100
What work still happens?

The simulation still evaluates charge response, periodic electrostatics, and interatomic forces. ALAMOS-0 removes iterative Krylov corrections in this tested configuration; its preconditioner was rebuilt every 5,000 steps.

THE KEY IDEA BEHIND SHADOW MD

Keep the forces conservative, even when the charge update is approximate.

Conventional Born–Oppenheimer dynamics minimizes electronic energy at each step. Shadow MD instead follows a nearby, exactly equilibrated energy surface, updated through auxiliary electronic variables. That gives well-defined conservative forces while avoiding repeated nonlinear minimization. ALAMOS accelerates the remaining charge-response work.

How I tested that claim ↗
03 / PHYSICAL VALIDATION

Fast isn't useful if the physics changes.

Eliminating corrective Krylov iterations is a major algorithmic result. The decisive next question is whether the resulting molecular trajectories preserve the physical behavior of the reference calculations. I implemented GJ-I Langevin dynamics, ran extended trajectories, checked thermal statistics, and calculated infrared spectra from dipole autocorrelations to answer that question.

✓
What the evidence supports

Across these tested water systems, shadow MD closely tracks tightly converged energies, maintains stable dynamics, and preserves the key temperature and IR signatures.

04 / WORK IN PROGRESS

What I'm building now.

The next challenge is making these algorithms general enough for other scientists to use, and reducing the cost of the long-range interactions that still remain.

SCIENTIFIC SOFTWARE / C++

General-purpose LAMMPS integration.

I implemented Shadow XL-BOMD (Levels 0/1) and ALAMOS-0 in a native C++/MPI LAMMPS development build, with multi-rank and restart tests passing. I am validating long-term stability and scalability ahead of integration into the open-source LAMMPS codebase.

VALIDATING FOR OPEN-SOURCE LAMMPS INTEGRATION
ALTERNATIVE ELECTROSTATICS / AMOS

Beyond global FFT-based electrostatics.

Charge updates are only part of the cost. I am exploring periodic electrostatics methods designed to avoid repeated global Fourier transforms and iterative long-range solves, with the broader goal of making flexible-charge simulations practical at costs approaching fixed-charge molecular dynamics.

NUMERICAL METHOD UNDER DEVELOPMENT
GENERAL NONLINEAR RESPONSE

Learning and simulating richer electronic response.

I am investigating how to reuse numerical work during nonlinear charge-response training, alongside active collaborative work on induced dipoles and charge-dependent D4 dispersion within broader flexible-response models.

CURRENT COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH
05 / WHERE THIS STARTED · 2025

Machine-learned materials, with charges that can change.

As 1 of 11 students selected for Texas A&M's research cohort, I developed a flexible-charge machine-learned potential for two-dimensional perovskites with Los Alamos National Laboratory mentorship. I checked predicted energies and charge distributions against density-functional-theory references. That work is where I first ran into the global charge-computation bottleneck.

MY FIRST RESEARCH PAPER

Shadow Molecular Dynamics for General Nonlinear Flexible-Charge Models

Available on arXivSubmitted to The Journal of Chemical Physics (JCP)

Jos Thomas · First author · 13 contributors · LANL–Sandia collaboration

General nonlinear flexible-charge models, accelerated through Shadow MD.

Developed with collaborators at Los Alamos National Laboratory and Sandia National Laboratories, our work establishes a general shadow molecular dynamics framework for nonlinear flexible-charge models with long-range electronic response. GPU simulations spanning more than 100,000 atoms demonstrate stable, scalable molecular dynamics with substantially less repeated charge equilibration.
